newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewish militant criticises Netanyahu over Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Jewish militant criticises Netanyahu over Hebron.

text.p: A Jewish militant leader of the outlawed anti-Arab Kach movement who lives in Hebron said on Friday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had no right to hand the West Bank town to Palestinian rule.

"At least half the state voted for Netanyahu in order that he would stop Hebron, the process in Hebron...Netanyahu has no right to implement the withdrawal in Hebron," Baruch Merzel told Israel Radio on Friday.
Netanyahu's government is locked in talks with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) on implementing a long-delayed troop redeployment in Hebron agreed to by Israel's previous government.
Netanyahu seeks to modify the Hebron deal to safeguard the 400 Jewish settlers who live in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs. Palestinians reject any changes to the accord.
Witnesses said Jewish visitors had begun to stream into Hebron late on Friday afternoon.
Hundreds of religious Jews were expected to join the Jewish community in Hebron over their sabbath, from Friday evening through Saturday evening.
Jews flock to the city every year during the sabbath in which they read the Bible portion relating the patriarch Abraham's purchase of a burial area in Hebron for his wife, Sarah.
The Tomb of the Patriarchs in Hebron, traditionally the site bought by Abraham, is now a complex revered by both Jews and Moslems. It is known to Moslems as the al-Ibrahimi mosque.
In February 1994 a Jewish militant from Kiryat Arba settlement adjacent to Hebron shot dead 29 Moslems at prayer in the mosque. He was beaten to death by survivors.
Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak confirmed on Friday that Israeli officials met on Thursday night to discuss how to deal with Jewish militants who might actively oppose turnover of Hebron.
Israel's Channel One Television asked Bazak how Netanyahu could take a "strong hand" against even a part of the right-wing public that had voted him into office.
"First of all, no one is about to take a strong hand with any side. Yesterday there was a discussion between the legal and security establishments that dicussed this issue," Bazak said.

"A strong hand is not directed against the right or the left, against this or that man. A strong hand, when necessary, is to be directed against someone who breaks the law and it is not connected to his political identification."
Israel's Haaretz newspaper said the meeting focused on issuing administrative detention orders which would allow security forces to imprison Jewish militants without trial.
Israel Television and radio early on Friday said such an order had already been issued against Merzel but the Israeli army denied the reports.

Merzel, who is under house arrest at his home in a fortified Jewish enclave in Hebron and has been held in administrative detention in the past, said his doing another stint in prison without trial might be a good thing.
"The public would wake up, understand who we're dealing with," Merzel told the radio.
